extracted.intended_audience: educators, NEA members, school administrators, education advocates, and legal counsel interested in federal and state legal developments affecting public education
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate whether federal and state executive actions, agency guidance, rulemaking, and litigation affecting K–12 and higher education comply with applicable statutes, constitutional provisions, and administrative law procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential/statutory authority for executive actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive actions must be authorized by the relevant statute; the President may not exercise powers beyond statutory grants (e.g., IEEPA does not authorize sweeping tariffs; procurement authority has limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether the President has statutory authority for an EO or policy. Examples: the Supreme Court held the President lacked power to impose sweeping tariffs under IEEPA; challenges to EOs (e.g., birthright citizenship EO, contractor DEI EO) focus on whether the cited statutory grant supports the action. The page notes courts are often split on the scope of delegation (e.g., procurement/statute authorizing economical and efficient contracting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) notice-and-comment and reasoned decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must follow APA rulemaking procedures — publish proposed rules, accept public comment, consider significant comments, and address them in the final rule; failures can invalidate regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA explains ED 'must follow notice-and-comment procedures' for rules like the proposed college accountability metric; failing to consider significant comments or rushing implementation (e.g., admissions data requirement described as 'rushed and chaotic') are grounds for APA challenges and injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious review / reasoned explanation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency actions that are arbitrary, capricious, or lacking reasoned explanation are unlawful under the APA and subject to vacatur or injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have struck or enjoined actions described as 'arbitrary and capricious'—examples include ED’s discontinuation of grants without required procedures, HHS Head Start changes, and other agency reorganizations adopted without adequate justification or analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spending Clause and appropriations restrictions on transferring funds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution vests spending power in Congress; agencies and the President cannot unilaterally transfer or reallocate appropriated funds in ways forbidden by appropriations statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA cites the FY 2026 appropriations act and congressional explanatory statements that prohibit ED from transferring appropriated funds to other agencies; interagency agreements and purported transfers of programs/funds (e.g., ED → DOL or ED → Treasury) risk violating appropriations law and the Spending Clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory assignment of program administration — cannot offload statutorily assigned duties
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute assigns program administration, an agency may not lawfully shift the program’s administrative and oversight obligations to another agency absent statutory authority or congressional approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Higher Education Act creates FSA within ED with oversight responsibilities; moving FSA functions to Treasury or shifting ED programs to HHS/State/DOL via interagency agreements conflicts with statutory assignments and appropriations restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX procedural safeguards before ending funding or rescinding agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Before rescinding federal funding or resolution agreements under Title IX, ED must follow required procedures (e.g., make findings, provide opportunity for voluntary compliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA notes a New York judge found ED unlawfully discontinued Magnet School Assistance Program grants because ED 'failed to follow required Title IX procedures (including findings and an opportunity for voluntary compliance)' and ordered funding restored. Withholding funds without following these procedures can be overturned.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA limits on parental access and no affirmative-notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: FERPA gives parents/legal guardians/adult students the right to access education records upon request but does not require schools to affirmatively notify parents of gender support plans or other records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ED used a Dear Colleague Letter to claim forced-outing-prevention policies may violate FERPA; NEA explains FERPA does not require affirmative notification and that ED’s findings based on third-party complaints (not parent requests) are legally suspect. Litigation is ongoing in several states.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment — viewpoint discrimination and compelled speech limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may not condition funding or contracts in ways that amount to viewpoint discrimination or compelled speech; using enforcement mechanisms (e.g., False Claims Act) to penalize disfavored viewpoints raises constitutional issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA flags constitutional problems with proposed GSA certification requirements and the contractor DEI EO, noting potential viewpoint discrimination, compelled speech, vagueness (Due Process), and First Amendment concerns. Plaintiffs argue EOs and certification rules that penalize DEI/particular viewpoints violate the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment — Establishment and Free Exercise constraints on religious expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions must be tested under Establishment and Free Exercise Clause principles (e.g., displays of the Ten Commandments, teacher prayer) and evaluated against Supreme Court precedent such as Kennedy v. Bremerton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page discusses the Fifth Circuit’s reliance on Kennedy v. Bremerton to uphold a Texas Ten Commandments law and warns ED guidance expanding when educators may pray at work stretches Kennedy and risks religious coercion. Challenges to religious-exercise claims turn on neutrality, general applicability, coercion, and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections Clause and limits on presidential action regarding federal elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Elections Clause vests primary authority for federal election 'Times, Places, and Manner' in the states (subject to congressional action); the President lacks power to unilaterally make rules relating to federal elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA treats the EO directing DHS/USPS to create voter lists and regulate mail-in ballots as likely unlawful, noting lawsuits allege violations of Article I, the First/Fifth/Tenth Amendments, the Voting Rights Act, the Privacy Act, and the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title VI—limits on federal reinterpretation to ban DEI programs
rubrics_metrics.description: ED’s position that Title VI prohibits programs promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion is inconsistent with statutory text and controlling precedent, making agency determinations under that theory vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA notes multiple courts have rejected the Administration’s position and that resolution agreements finding Title VI violations for partnerships (e.g., with The Ph.D. Project) are likely unfounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption in immigration-related education policy
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws affecting immigration-adjacent education matters (e.g., in-state tuition for undocumented students) may be preempted by federal immigration law depending on statutory conflict and field preemption doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOJ sued Nebraska claiming the state’s in-state tuition law is preempted; courts have reached differing outcomes (e.g., dismissal in Minnesota, consent decrees in some states), so preemption analysis is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR statutory duty to investigate and resolve civil rights complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office for Civil Rights (OCR) must 'effectuate' federal civil rights laws in ED-funded programs and, under its regulations, promptly investigate and resolve civil rights complaints rather than dismissing them without investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO found OCR dismissed a high percentage of complaints without investigation after staff reductions; NEA and partners have sued alleging the workforce reductions and resulting dismissals render OCR unable to fulfill statutory obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency guidance cannot rewrite statutes or overrule judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s guidance cannot change statutory text or overturn court interpretations; parties may challenge guidance that purports to alter statutory rights (e.g., Title IX protections for transgender students).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEA emphasizes that Title IX protections 'should be understood to extend to transgender students under existing legal precedent,' and that ED cannot change the statute or overrule court decisions merely by issuing guidance or rescinding agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness and pre-enforcement/injunction considerations in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider procedural defects (rushed adoption, failure to respond to comments, lack of reasoned analysis) and equities (irreparable harm, likelihood of success) when granting stays, preliminary injunctions, or vacatur of agency actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include injunctions blocking ED’s admissions data requirement for being rapidly adopted without adequate public process, preliminary injunctions restoring bargaining rights, and injunctions blocking withholding of funds where ED failed to follow required procedures or lacked clear legal bases.
